title: Psychology of Human Relationships Adventure 3: Bystander Effect & Pro-social Behaviour
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet Latané & Darley's bystander effect and the roots of pro-social action.
meta_desc: Psychology Human Relationships: bystander effect (Latané & Darley 1968) and pro-social behaviour.
final_note: You explained the bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility.

concepts.def: Help less likely with more witnesses

walkthroughs.body_html:
After the 1964 Kitty Genovese case (later evidence revised the story), John Darley & Bibb Latané studied bystander apathy.

Smoke-filled room (1968): when alone, 75% reported smoke; in a group of three, only 38%.

Seizure study (1968): with one perceived bystander, 85% helped; with four, only 31%.

Latané & Darley's five-stage decision model:

1. Notice the event.
2. Interpret as an emergency.
3. Take responsibility.
4. Decide what to do.
5. Act.

Two key processes: diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance.

Daniel Batson (1991) empathy-altruism hypothesis: empathy creates genuine altruistic motivation — not just self-soothing.

Encouraging help: training in noticing, naming individuals ('You in the red shirt — call 911'), modelling helping, reducing anonymity.
